It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while witnessing the “noise and tumult” of a world that measures your worth by a “string of degrees” or a “balanced checkbook,” and I must ask you with a gentle spirit: why do you ask after the nature of economic instability and the withering of your heart in this hour? [10, 391, 1503, 1605, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” because the “statistics” of a “free and prosperous society” offer you only “spiritual placebos” that cannot reach the “horrible pit” of your anxiety, or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor your soul in the truth that the Master “sovereignly orders everything He has made”—including the rise and fall of markets? [1, 13, 20, 31, 114, 148, 1143, 1532, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many “shave off the edges” of the truth to suggest that human success is a sign of divine blessing, we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Lord personally governs the “vicissitudes of life” by demanding that we “examine everything carefully” within our own hearts [1, 11, 28, 116, 1313, 1503, 1515, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, your feeling of precarity is not an “administrative anomaly” but a “test to prove your virtue” by a Father who “knows that you need all these things” [15, 59, 68, 1143, 1224, 1532, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: The Mirage of Statistical Prosperity**

**Verse**
“ ‘And He said to them, “Take heed and beware of covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses” ’ ” (Luke 12:15). [298, 1222, 1341, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Reformed theology—echoed by **John MacArthur**—warns that when “programs, methods, and money produce impressive results,” there is a great danger to “confuse human success with divine blessing” [1, 10, Conversation History]. Scripture reveals that the “wicked boast of his heart’s desire” and “bless the greedy,” yet their “glory... will vanish—like smoke they vanish away” (Psalm 10:3; 37:20) [43, 1411, 1684, Conversation History]. The “statistics” of the world are often a “spirit of fraud,” for the “unregenerate mind” thinks it is “rich, has become wealthy, and has need of nothing” while being “wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17) [505, 1151, 1523, Conversation History]. True flourishing is found not in “unrighteous mammon” but in a “heart prepared to receive the word,” for “the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17) [206, 322, 1154, 1406, 1670, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “not be deceived” by a “worldly philosophy” that suggests financial stability is the same as spiritual health, for “no slave can serve two masters” and you must “not love the world or the things in the world” (Matthew 6:24; 1 John 2:15) [91, 330, 487, 1502, 1553, 1624, Conversation History]. Recognize that “your life is not your own” because you were “bought at a price,” and your “sole objective” is to “seek first the kingdom of God,” knowing that “He will take care of all our needs” (1 Corinthians 6:20; Matthew 6:33) [12, 26, 101, 435, 1138, 1262, 1406, 1670, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Temporal Signs vs. Spiritual Reality**
In the ancient **Jewish context**, “national greatness” and “large and beautiful cities” were often seen as “temporal signs” of God’s favor under the Mosaic Law (Deuteronomy 28:1–14) [409, 1313, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** this by showing that the “church militant” is an “assembly of the citizens of heaven” whose “inheritance is incorruptible,” for “Jesus answered, ‘My kingdom is not of this world’ ” (1 Peter 1:4; John 18:36) [13, 26, 142, 830, 1313, 1426, 1529, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: The Heart "Struck Down Like Grass"**

**Verse**
“My heart is stricken and withered like grass, so that I forget to eat my bread. Because of my loud groaning my bones cling to my skin. I am like a pelican of the wilderness; I am like an owl of the desert” (Psalm 102:4–6). [144, 1126, 1315, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed pastoral tradition—echoed by **Charles Spurgeon**—acknowledges that the “horrible pit” of despair can strike even the “faithful servant,” for “Jeremiah lived the majority of his life in frustration and confusion, all the while weeping” (Lamentations 1:20) [11, 31, 1440, Conversation History]. When your heart feels “stricken like grass,” it is a “plain indication of God’s righteous judgment” used to “peel away the flesh and drive you to Himself” (2 Thessalonians 1:5) [63, Conversation History]. This “momentary, light affliction” is not evidence of abandonment, for “the Lord will respond to the prayer of the destitute” and “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (Psalm 102:17; 147:3) [144, 148, 479, 1033, 1122, Conversation History]. God allows the “withering” to prove that “all flesh is as grass,” but “the Word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:6, 8) [11, 121, 1306, 1413, 1684, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Trade in your worry for trust,” recognizing that “when anxiety was great within me, Your consolation brought joy to my soul” (Psalm 94:19) [90, 94, 144, 201, 1033, 1113, 1408, 1515, Conversation History]. You must “discipline your mind” to “not lose heart,” for “He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6) [5, 113, 116, 829, 938, 1406, 1408, 1709, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Lament as Worship**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, “distress” was often met with “sackcloth and ashes” as a sign of “sorrow of heart” (Esther 4:1) [832, 928, 1118, 1463, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “spiritual service of worship,” teaching that we can “boldly say: ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear. What can man do to me?’ ” because we have an “anchor of the soul” within the veil (Hebrews 13:6; 6:19) [4, 450, 826, 934, 1235, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: God’s Sovereignty over Financial Precarity**

**Verse**
“ ‘The LORD makes poor and makes rich; He brings low and lifts up. He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the beggar from the ash heap, to set them among princes and make them inherit the throne of glory’ ” (1 Samuel 2:7–8). [716, 940, 1015, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Scripture handles the “vicissitudes of life” by affirming that God “positively ordains whatsoever comes to pass,” including “market highs” and personal “needs” [122, 1143, 1429, 1497, 1565, Conversation History]. God “harnesses the deeds of the wicked” and the “choices” of men to fulfill His “one continuous plan of redemption,” for “the silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, says the LORD of hosts” (Haggai 2:8) [5, 327, 1132, 1406, 1429, 1515, 1567, 1616, Conversation History]. Whether you are in “abundance” or “suffer lack,” every “good gift” is a “lavish endowment” from the Father, and “He will not let your foot slip” (James 1:17; Psalm 121:3) [36, 146, 244, 252, 841, 1095, 1339, Conversation History]. Your “precarity” is subject to the “determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God,” ensuring that “nothing thwarts any aspect of His plan” (Acts 2:23) [5, 1132, 1431, 1503, 1567, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Wait for His Son from heaven,” knowing that “the Lord has established His throne in heaven, and His kingdom rules over all” (Psalm 103:19) [15, 24, 94, 201, 1143, 1408, 1515, 1532, Conversation History]. You should find “tranquility of soul” by “committing your works to the LORD,” for “your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (Proverbs 16:3; 1 Corinthians 15:58) [101, 192, 201, 368, 483, 1221, 1315, 1408, 1515, 1670, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Sovereignty over the Despot**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, God used “hostile nations” as a “rod of My anger” to test His people (Isaiah 10:5) [717, 740, 924, 1110, 1316, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our view, revealing that even the “worst atrocity ever carried out”—the Cross—was the means of our “victory,” proving that God can use economic “calamity” to “perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle” His chosen ones (1 Peter 5:10) [5, 93, 116, 213, 811, 1143, 1408, 1431, 1515, 1567, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 4: The Settled Certainty of the New Jerusalem**

**Verse**
“ ‘And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; there shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying. There shall be no more pain, for the former things have passed away’ ” (Revelation 21:4). [14, 201, 468, 470, 645, 816, 940, 948, 1315, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The biblical authors resolve the “noise and tumult” of earthly instability by fixating on the “consummation of history,” where “Christ ultimately crushes the kingdoms of men and establishes His own” [13, 20, 24, 103, 136, 1199, 1315, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. Our “hope” is rooted in a “city whose builder and maker is God,” an “inheritance incorruptible and undefiled” that no “famine” or “economic siege” can touch (Hebrews 11:10; 1 Peter 1:4) [13, 26, 142, 830, 1251, 1313, 1426, 1470, 1515, 1592, Conversation History]. The Reformed tradition—echoed by **Voddie Baucham**—asserts that “scars... don’t define us; our hope does,” for we wait for a world where “the Lord God will illumine them” and “they will reign forever” (Revelation 22:5) [432, 484, 647, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Trade in your worry for trust,” for “the heavens will pass away with a great noise... but the Word of our God stands forever” (2 Peter 3:10; Isaiah 40:8) [11, 21, 94, 121, 324, 1306, 1408, 1515, 1684, Conversation History]. Your “true identity” is “hid with Christ in God,” so “do not let your heart be troubled,” for the King has already “overcome the world” (Colossians 3:3; John 14:1; 16:33) [12, 13, 14, 24, 31, 68, 92, 101, 102, 131, 142, 190, 243, 248, 252, 483, 666, 776, 1032, 1036, 1136, 1138, 1262, 1313, 1406, 1426, 1515, 1646, 1670, Conversation History].

***

**Final Reminder**
“Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19). [11, 87, 147, 176, 211, 222, 285, 300, 313, 324, 332, 361, 405, 413, 414, 444, 449, 591, 1138, 1407, 1441, 1450, Conversation History].

references.cited_text: Daniel was often in dangerous situations because of his strategic role within the pagan Babylonian society. In his concern over Judah’s captivity, he prayed, “Alas, O Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant and lovingkindness for those who love Him and keep His commandments, we have sinned” (Dan. 9:4–5). He began his prayer by affirming the nature and character of God. The prophet Jeremiah lived the majority of his life in frustration and confusion, all the while weeping with a broken heart over his people. While he could have easily despaired over his ministry, he never became preoccupied with his own painful circumstances. Instead he would pray and extol the glory, name, and works of God (e.g., Jer. 32:17–23).

Anxiety is, at its core, an inappropriate response in light of circumstances; it’s very different from the cares and concerns in life that cause people to attend to business in a responsible way. Stress and pressure, instead of being things to avoid, strengthen us to accomplish the challenges God sets before us in life. The apostle Paul wrote that apart from the unrelenting external pressures he had to face, such as persecution, hardship, and imprisonment, he also had daily upon him the internal pressure “of concern for all the churches” (2 Cor. 11:28). In spite of that, he had room in his heart to feel the anxiety of others, for he went on to write, “Who is weak without my being weak? Who is led into sin without my intense concern?” (v. 29). He wouldn’t have had it any other way, though. In fact, that kind of response to pressure was what Paul looked for in those who would serve with him. Note how he commended Timothy to the Philippian church: “I have no one else of kindred spirit who will genuinely be concerned for your welfare” (Phil. 2:20; cf. 1 Cor. 4:17).
